Most courses define academic integrity by authorship: the work is yours if you wrote it.
The independent project does not work that way.
An AI agent will write most of your code, and that is the assignment, not a loophole.

What makes the project yours is everything the agent cannot do for you.
You decide what to build.
You direct the work and judge what comes back.
You put in the hours, and you come away understanding what you made.
Not every line of it—nobody expects you to recall a generated helper function months later—but what your app does, how it fits together, and why it is built the way it is.

So dishonesty here is not a question of who typed the code.
It is a question of whether you misrepresented your own engagement.
A good test:
if you can sit down with a tutor and walk them through your app—what it does, why it is built that way, what you tried that didn’t work—you are fine.

The standard
University of Illinois academic integrity policies
apply to the independent project, including your Claude Code session transcripts and the activity your Claude Code hooks report as you work.
Here is how each category of infraction applies:

Cheating:
Having someone else conduct Claude Code sessions on your behalf or otherwise complete your project work for you.

Plagiarism:
Directly copying another student’s code or Claude Code session logs and presenting them as your own.

Fabrication:
Editing, manufacturing, or otherwise tampering with Claude Code session logs, or with the activity your Claude Code hooks report, to misrepresent work you didn’t actually do. This includes using your project sessions for unrelated work, or any other attempt to inflate your measured hours.

Facilitation:
Sharing your Claude Code session transcripts, repository access, or verification codes with another student so they can submit your work as theirs.

Bribes, favors, and threats:
Attempting to influence project grading through inappropriate means.

Academic interference:
Tampering with another student’s repository, session transcripts, or project materials.

We will run automated checks on reported session activity, session transcripts, and code changes.
Evidence of any of the above will initiate academic integrity proceedings under the same policies described in our

Using AI in this course is optional. You can complete every assignment and earn full marks without ever using an AI
tool. If you do use one, the rules in this policy apply.

The Standard

Our course standard is this: you must write your own code, and you must be able to explain every line of it. If a
course staff member asks why you wrote a particular line, what a specific variable represents, or how a section of
your code works, you should be able to answer immediately and confidently, without consulting any resource; if you
cannot, you have not yet learned what the assignment was designed to teach, regardless of whether your code
compiles and passes test cases. Stated as a rule of use, AI may support your process, e.g., understanding the
problem, learning relevant concepts, developing a strategy, debugging your attempts, and verifying correctness, but
it may not produce your product, i.e., the code you submit, which you must be able to reproduce independently.

Permitted Uses

You may use AI tools to assist your work on graded lessons, recitation activities, and machine problems in the
following ways:

Breaking down assignments:
Ask the AI to help you understand what an assignment is asking,
identify the component parts of the problem, and clarify requirements that seem ambiguous.

Developing a problem-solving plan:
Use the AI to help you formulate a high-level approach
before you begin writing code; that is, discuss algorithmic strategies, consider edge cases, and think through
the logical structure of your solution.

Explaining concepts or syntax:
When you encounter unfamiliar C++ constructs, language
features, or programming concepts, use the AI to help make sense of them.

cryptic. The AI can help you interpret what went wrong and why.

AI tool
is any generative system that produces code, text, or
explanations in response to a prompt, however you access it: through a chat interface, an editor extension, a
command-line tool, or an agent. Dictionaries, translation tools, spell checkers, and non-generative editor
completion are not AI tools under this policy and are always permitted. During a quiz, no tool beyond what the
testing environment provides falls within any permitted use. The governing prohibition appears under

Quiz Environment and Conduct
.

Using AI in this course is optional. You can complete every assignment and earn full marks without ever using an AI
tool. If you do use one, the rules in this policy apply.

The Standard

Our course standard is this: you must write your own code, and you must be able to explain every line of it. If a
course staff member asks why you wrote a particular line, what a specific variable represents, or how a section of
your code works, you should be able to answer immediately and confidently, without consulting any resource; if you
cannot, you have not yet learned what the assignment was designed to teach, regardless of whether your code
compiles and passes test cases. Stated as a rule of use, AI may support your process, e.g., understanding the
problem, learning relevant concepts, developing a strategy, debugging your attempts, and verifying correctness, but
it may not produce your product, i.e., the code you submit, which you must be able to reproduce independently.

Permitted Uses

You may use AI tools to assist your work on graded lessons, recitation activities, and machine problems in the
following ways:

Breaking down assignments:
Ask the AI to help you understand what an assignment is asking,
identify the component parts of the problem, and clarify requirements that seem ambiguous.

Developing a problem-solving plan:
Use the AI to help you formulate a high-level approach
before you begin writing code; that is, discuss algorithmic strategies, consider edge cases, and think through
the logical structure of your solution.

Explaining concepts or syntax:
When you encounter unfamiliar C++ constructs, language
features, or programming concepts, use the AI to help make sense of them.

Understanding error messages and debugging output:
Compiler errors and runtime failures can be
cryptic. The AI can help you interpret what went wrong and why.

Reviewing and explaining code:
After you have written code yourself, use the AI t

statements.anchor: This course seeks to impart and measure a solid understanding of course material
statements.label: course measures understanding not prompting
statements.passage:
Generative AI tools can provide plausible text or code, but they do not replace your learning. This course seeks to impart and measure a solid understanding of course material rather than your knack in prompting a model.

Improper use of AI tools can:

Mask gaps in your understanding

Lead to incorrect or unverified solutions

Cause poor performance in unplugged exams and interviews

Warning
WARNING

AI usage is not allowed in individual assessments (i.e., quizzes and exams). Any use of AI tools in these assements is a breach of class policy.

That said, we recognize that generative AI tools can be useful for brainstorming, ideation and additional learning. You may sparingly use generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Bard) to assist your learning and problem solving.

We strongly recommend a maximal attempt to solving problems yourself before resorting to LLM use.

Your AI usage in this class is subject to the following guidelines:

You must re-write:
all solutions, code, explanations based solely on
your understanding
without help after AI usage.

Simply copying text or code from an AI tool into your submission (even with attribution) is
NOT
acceptable.

Simply reading the AI generated solution is
NOT
learning.

Simply paraphrasing the AI solution while having it open is
NOT
based on
your understanding.
Go for a run, have a meal – come back and then redo the problem
by yourself
.

While we won’t enforce this guideline any deviation from it will naturally become obvious (see point 3 above).

Like Prof. Erickson
writes
,
“…
Understanding
is a seductive lie, a warm feeling of satisfaction that your brain uses as a defense mechanism against doing real work. The only way to know when
when
you truly understand the concepts (is) when you can do the work.”

So, if after using AI, you cannot solve a problem of the same pattern on your own, you have
not
learned the material.

You must clearly document usage of the tool
: On any submitted work where AI usage is allowed, include a short statement at the top or bottom of your submission. For example:

Used ChatGPT (GPT-4) to help interpret problem prompt and brainstorm
approaches; final solution written entirely in my own words."

Treat AI assistance like any other external source
: Use it to inform your work instead of generating it.
Always validate it independently.
Then, cite any usage, and describe/reflect on how you used it to inform your work or better your understanding.

Generative AI tools can provide plausible text or code, but they do not replace your learning. This course seeks to impart and measure a solid understanding of course material rather than your knack in prompting a model.

Improper use of AI tools can:

Mask gaps in your understanding

Lead to incorrect or unverified solutions

Cause poor performance in unplugged exams and interviews

Warning
WARNING

AI usage is not allowed in individual assessments (i.e., quizzes and exams). Any use of AI tools in these assements is a breach of class policy.

That said, we recognize that generative AI tools can be useful for brainstorming, ideation and additional learning. You may sparingly use generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Bard) to assist your learning and problem solving.

We strongly recommend a maximal attempt to solving problems yourself before resorting to LLM use.

Your AI usage in this class is subject to the following guidelines:

You must re-write:
all solutions, code, explanations based solely on
your understanding
without help after AI usage.

Simply copying text or code from an AI tool into your submission (even with attribution) is
NOT
acceptable.

Simply reading the AI generated solution is
NOT
learning.

Simply paraphrasing the AI solution while having it open is
NOT
based on
your understanding.
Go for a run, have a meal – come back and then redo the problem
by yourself
.

While we won’t enforce this guideline any deviation from it will naturally become obvious (see point 3 above).

Like Prof. Erickson
writes
,
“…
Understanding
is a seductive lie, a warm feeling of satisfaction that your brain uses as a defense mechanism against doing real work. The only way to know when
when
you truly understand the concepts (is) when you can do the work.”

So, if after using AI, you cannot solve a problem of the same pattern on your own, you have
not
learned the material.

You must clearly document usage of the tool
: On any submitted work where AI usage is allowed, include a short statement at the top or bottom of your submission. For example:

Used ChatGPT (GPT-4) to help interpret problem prompt and brainstorm
approaches; final solution written entirely in my own words."

Treat AI assistance like any other external source
: Use it to inform your work instead of generating it.
Always validate it independently.
Then, cite any usage, and describe/reflect on how you used it to inform your work or better your understanding.

statements.passage:
Recent advances in generative AI require us to adapt the way in which we teach and assess students
in all disciplines of computer science. Current coding agents such as Codex or Claude can produce
fully working artifacts for structured course projects with little or no human intervention, solely on
the basis of detailed specifications like the ones we typically prepare for such projects. As a result,
we must minimize longer use code artifacts created in unproctored environments to assess the skills
or level of mastery of students.
That said, we continue to believe that projects that require you to apply the systems-level concepts
you’re exposed to in the context of specific requirements, environments, and system designs, and
that result in deliverables are very likely to be beneficial, if not necessary, to achieve the level of
skills and understanding of systems we (and future employers) expect CS graduates to possess.
For this reason, our approach is fourfold:
1. We continue to include projects that are designed to be implemented by humans with minimal
or no AI support.
2. We will allow the use of AI assistants for these projects, but (not yet) require their use.

There are no restrictions regarding the use of generative AI tools for generating or
debugging code.
That said, we advise that you be careful in their use. No matter how sophisticated AI tools become,
it is the valueyou provide, not them, that ultimately determines whether you will be attractive to
future employers. It is likely that employers will continue to assess job candidates in unassisted or
minimally assisted scenarios, in addition to testing their assisted AI skills.
For this reason, students remain fully responsible for the accuracy, originality, and integrity of all
submitted work. Furthermore, we may require you to explain, defend, revise, or orally demonstrate
any AI-assisted submission.
Although we allow the use of AI for generating code (and debugging tasks), we do not allow their use
for impersonation in contexts where you are expected to represent your own mind and personality.
In particular, the creation of discussion posts using generative AI isforbidden without proper
attribution/quotation that clearly delineates your (human) contribution and that of AI. If you
contribute AI-generated material, you must clearly attribute it and augment it with your own
contribution.

Policy on Use of Generative AI

In general, we will treat the use of generative AI the same as we would a student asking for help on StackOverflow or finding other sources of code. For coding questions (i.e. “How do I make Google login work with Django?”), students are welcome to use generative AI. WeI suggest trying it!)

For artifact documents and other writing prompts, generative AI is discouraged and honestly won’t be of too much help regardless. While these tools can give you some impressive boilerplate text that would work for a generic presentation, it’s not going to have the specific details of what your team had to do to make your project a success, and that’s what we are specifically assessing. So, if you lean too heavily on generative AI, your submission isn’t going to earn much XP (if any) because we really don’t want to read a bunch of generic “why is devops good” sort of text. We care a lot more about how your team was impacted.

Unless otherwise specified, all graded work must be completed individually, and AI tools (such as ChatGPT, CoPilot, Gemini, etc.) should not be used on graded work in any way.

In particular, all graded work must abide by these rules:

Do not share solution code with, or view solution code from, any sources, including but not limited to fellow students, prior students, tutors, or the internet.

Do not provide or receive detailed guidance on, such as being “walked through” or “walking someone through”, how to implement any part of a graded assignment to or from anyone who is not a member of the course staff.

Do not provide or view samples of code that are intended to solve any specific part of a graded assignment’s specification, unless the samples are included in course-provided or course-linked materials.

Do not use AI in relation to your graded work in a manner not allowed by the course

statements.anchor: allows the use of AI to help understand core concepts or clarify misconceptions
statements.label: AI allowed to understand concepts
statements.passage:
As AI tools become more widely available and more widely used in software development, it is becoming more difficult to teach an introductory computing course without acknowledging the existence of these tools. For this reason, we are using a new AI policy in
CSE 123
that allows the use of AI to help understand core concepts or clarify misconceptions, but emphasizes that all work submitted for a grade must be entirely your own.

While this policy allows limited use of AI tools,
you do not
need
to use AI to succeed in
CSE 123
.

The
CSE 123
policy on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools is summarized as follows:

No part of any graded work may touch an AI tool.

You may not copy and paste any work generated by AI into any graded submission, nor may you copy and paste any work from or for a graded assignment into an AI tool. All other uses of AI tools on graded work must be cited.

“graded work”
means work that will be submitted for a grade, and includes both code and non-code text (e.g. reflection responses).

“copy and paste”
includes manually re-typing text.

“AI tool”
means
any
interface that uses AI, including standalone large language model (LLM) chat platforms (e.g. ChatGPT) and ‘built-in’ or ‘plugin’ AI tools (e.g. GitHub Copilot).

The following are examples of allowed and prohibited uses of AI according to this policy:

Allowed

Asking AI to explain an error message (but not to provide a fix)

Asking AI to explain the functionality of a provided code snippet that is
not
part of graded work

Asking AI to suggest additional information or resources related to a reflection prompt (but not to write a reflection for you)

Prohibited

Generating code, comments, reflections, or any other work for an assignment

Using AI to ‘solve’ (part of) an assignment

Using AI to write, modify, or extend assignment reflections, code, comments, etc.

This policy is grounded in a belief that AI tools can provide value when used responsibly, but that it is also important to first learn the fundamental skills that we are teaching
without
the use of these tools. There are too many possible uses of AI to enumerate them all, but we have attempted to provide representative examples. When in doubt, please feel free to ask for clarification. If you believe the policy disallows something that should be allowed, please let us know via email or the
anonymous feedback form
.

Citing Use of AI
¶

In accordance with the AI policy above, you are required to cite any use of AI

policy on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools is summarized as follows:

No part of any graded work may touch an AI tool.

You may not copy and paste any work generated by AI into any graded submission, nor may you copy and paste any work from or for a graded assignment into an AI tool. All other uses of AI tools on graded work must be cited.

“graded work”
means work that will be submitted for a grade, and includes both code and non-code text (e.g. reflection responses).

“copy and paste”
includes manually re-typing text.

“AI tool”
means
any
interface that uses AI, including standalone large language model (LLM) chat platforms (e.g. ChatGPT) and ‘built-in’ or ‘plugin’ AI tools (e.g. GitHub Copilot).

Allowed

Asking AI to explain an error message (but not to provide a fix)

Asking AI to explain the functionality of a provided code snippet that is

Prohibited

What is Generative AI?

Generative AI refers to a kind of artifical intelligence software
that is capable of getting information in response to prompts.
The software is trained on source data, and uses that training data
as input to a sophisticated model that predicts the appropriate
response to the prompt.
It does not understand the prompts, but it produces a convincing
simulation of understanding.
Examples of generative AI systems that use text include ChatGPT and
Bard, and generative AI models capable of generating images include
Midjourney and DALL-E.

Risks of Generative AI

Accuracy:
If you are using generative AI tools
for learning then you should always double-check the content.
For example, if you are assigned to write a program that uses a
specific algorithm, AI tools may generate a solution that arrives
at the correct answer but does not use the required algorithm.
If you use generative AI to assist in the creation of assessed
content then you are responsible for the accuracy and correctness
of the work that you submit.

Quality:
Content generated may be of poor quality,
and generic in nature.
Code may have security flaws and may contain bugs.
It is important that you understand how any generated code works
and you evaluate the quality of the content.

Learning:
Generative AI can be a powerful productivity
tool for users who are already familiar with the topic of the
generated content because they can evaluate and revise the
content as appropriate.
Tasks assigned by your teachers are designed to help you learn,
and relying on AI tools to complete tasks denies you the
opportunity to learn, and to receive accurate feedback on your
learning.

Over-reliance:
Using AI tools to do your work for you
may achieve the short-term goal of assignment completion, but
consistent over-reliance on AI tools may prevent you from being
prepared for later examinations, subsequent coursework, or
future job opportunities.

Motivation:
Some students may experience lack of
motivation for task

What is Generative AI?

Generative AI refers to a kind of artifical intelligence software
that is capable of getting information in response to prompts.
The software is trained on source data, and uses that training data
as input to a sophisticated model that predicts the appropriate
response to the prompt.
It does not understand the prompts, but it produces a convincing
simulation of understanding.
Examples of generative AI systems that use text include ChatGPT and
Bard, and generative AI models capable of generating images include
Midjourney and DALL-E.

Risks of Generative AI

Accuracy:
If you are using generative AI tools
for learning then you should always double-check the content.
For example, if you are assigned to write a program that uses a
specific algorithm, AI tools may generate a solution that arrives
at the correct answer but does not use the required algorithm.
If you use generative AI to assist in the creation of assessed
content then you are responsible for the accuracy and correctness
of the work that you submit.

Quality:
Content generated may be of poor quality,
and generic in nature.
Code may have security flaws and may contain bugs.
It is important that you understand how any generated code works
and you evaluate the quality of the content.

Learning:
Generative AI can be a powerful productivity
tool for users who are already familiar with the topic of the
generated content because they can evaluate and revise the
content as appropriate.

learning.

prepared for later examinations, subsequent coursework, or
